extracted.intended_audience: mathematics faculty, teacher educators, program designers, and prospective middle-school mathematics teachers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive standards for creating, running, and evaluating middle-school mathematics teacher-preparation programs (course composition, pedagogy, assessment, licensure alignment, and capstone requirements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Program course composition (UWO middle school program)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students complete Number Systems, Geometry and Measurement, Data Exploration and Analysis, three of four mathematics electives (Modern Algebra, Modern Geometry, Infinite Processes, Probability and Statistics), and a 3-credit capstone Senior Seminar for a total of 24 credit hours of mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each of the four 4-credit electives is designed specifically for future middle grades teachers and only students in the middle school program take them. Provide sample syllabi links and require a coherent bundle of core + electives + capstone tailored to middle grades teachers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerequisite requirement for program entry
rubrics_metrics.description: A grade of C or better in Intermediate Algebra is prerequisite to the Number Systems course and is thus a prerequisite for the program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit course prerequisite(s) should be stated to ensure readiness for program content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensable minor / endorsement GPA requirement (Wisconsin)
rubrics_metrics.description: In Wisconsin, the program constitutes a licensable minor. Students must earn a 3.0 GPA in the courses in order to obtain that endorsement on their teaching licenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track and enforce the GPA threshold required by state licensure rules; document requirement in program materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical culture and values as program aim
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the culture of mathematicians (values, mathematical tools, and distinctions about language) transparent to students: valuing problems, careful definitions, deductive arguments, shared notation, logic, examples/counterexamples, extreme/trivial cases, modeling, attention to quantifiers and precise language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design courses and classroom practices to expose students to these cultural practices explicitly (language use, argumentation norms, model-building).

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructivist pedagogical stance
rubrics_metrics.description: Program is constructivist: 'knowledge must be conceived by the learner' and learning is 'a model of participating in a culture rather than a model of transmitting knowledge.' The program is designed to support mathematizing as a practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Course design should facilitate student-generated conceptions, prior-meaning activation, participation in mathematical practice, and activities that support mathematizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teacher-educator role and classroom discourse practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Teachers should be prepared to 'give commentary from the perspective of one who could judge which aspects of the children’s activity might be mathematically significant', initiate shifts in discourse, develop symbolic records of contributions, and frame whole-class discussions of obligations and expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model these practices in courses; require students to practice judging significance, facilitating discourse shifts, and recording contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Activity-based elective design
rubrics_metrics.description: Elective content courses are activity-based and designed to encourage deep understandings and the mathematical thinking of children; courses require students to practice mathematically powerful ways of thinking, speaking, and behaving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use small-group work followed by whole-class discussion; design activities that lead to 'Read and Study' sections, 'Connections' to middle school curriculum, and homework that are not mere exercises but problems to be thought of from a teacher's perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructor non-intervention norm during student problem solving
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructors refrain from giving answers or participating overtly in the problem-solving process; they 'watch and listen' as students work and only lead whole-class discussions after students have attempted tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a policy of minimal instructor intervention during group discovery to allow sense-making; use post-attempt whole-class synthesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis on reading and using mathematical definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to read and then use a new mathematical definition is part of learning how to learn mathematics; fostering such skills is an explicit aim of the program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include activities explicitly aimed at reading, interpreting, and applying definitions (e.g., algebra activity to learn binary operation definition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Significant written work and explanation of reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Courses require significant written work: assignments typically ask students to describe problem-solving strategies as well as solutions and to make mathematical arguments that solutions are correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require written explanations, proofs or arguments, and reflective writing connecting solutions to pedagogy; grade for clarity and justification, not just final answers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Project-based assignments relating math content to history or education
rubrics_metrics.description: Each course requires a project in which students relate course content to its historical development or to educational issues (e.g., reading research and interviewing children, categorizing thinking via theoretical frameworks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a substantive project with public presentation to class; provide expectations and rubrics linking content knowledge to pedagogical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment variety (exams, quizzes, homework, projects, presentations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students are assessed using written exams, quizzes, homework assignments, projects, and presentations; presentations provide practice preparing, explaining, and listening to mathematical ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a mix of formative and summative assessments that evaluate procedural skill, conceptual understanding, communicative ability, and pedagogical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern Algebra course goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand the language of algebra and logic; the structure of operations on sets; elementary group theory; power of pattern-seeking, modeling, and functional representations; and the nature of building and solving equations and systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design course materials to emphasize symbolizing, generalizing patterns, modeling with functions, and algebraic structure relevant to middle grades.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern Geometry course goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Demand that students think spatially, see structure in art and form, and create and visualize new worlds with different rules; explore axiom systems, classical Euclidean geometry through synthetic/analytic/transformational approaches, non-Euclidean geometries, and elementary topology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include hands-on tools (geoboards, mirrors, shape blocks), explorations of multiple geometries, and activities that link geometric ideas to middle-school standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinite Processes (intuition of calculus) goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide an intuitive approach to infinity, limits, continuity, derivative, definite integral, and the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus; explore paradoxes, countable/uncountable sets, infinite sequences and series, rates of change, and accumulation functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach ideas qualitatively and via examples that connect to middle-grade topics (e.g., decimal representations as infinite series).

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability and Statistics course goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach vocabulary and conceptual foundations of probability, data analysis, counting, and statistical inference; weave history of ideas and use real data whenever possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize data literacy, simulations, real-data projects, and connections to civic/statistical reasoning for middle grades.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capstone seminar structure and core questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Senior Seminar is a 3-credit seminar designed around three questions: (1) What is mathematics and mathematical behavior? (2) How do humans learn mathematics? (3) How should mathematics be taught?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Center capstone around readings (mathematicians and educational theorists), class discussion, panels (e.g., mathematicians), reflective writing, research papers, and curriculum projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research paper expectations in capstone
rubrics_metrics.description: Research papers must be related to the central questions of the course and supported by scholarly research literature; students are expected to read, analyze, and understand articles from peer-reviewed journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require citation of peer-reviewed literature, methodological awareness, and clear linkage of research to classroom practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curriculum project evaluation criteria (capstone)
rubrics_metrics.description: Team assessments of a reform-based middle-school curriculum unit must be based on the unit’s compatibility with constructivist theory, the NCTM Standards and the research literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During presentation, classmates evaluate lessons. Evaluation criteria include: importance and accuracy of mathematical content; use of mathematical processes (problem solving, communication, reasoning and proof); and the team’s use of their peers’ thinking and misconceptions during the presentation. Use iterative project cycles so feedback informs revisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recruitment and target student profile
rubrics_metrics.description: Program targets students who may not fare well as traditional mathematics majors but are bright, demonstrate aptitude for mathematical thought processes, and show eagerness to understand math better; recruit promising elementary education majors into middle school track.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively recruit from initial course sequences; use admissions and advising to identify candidates with potential rather than only those with extensive prior coursework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program outcomes tracking
rubrics_metrics.description: Track alumni outcomes (e.g., between 2005–2010, 144 completers; of 65 respondents 89% are currently employed as teachers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect and report placement and career data to evaluate program effectiveness; use response rates and context when interpreting statistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment with state licensure requirements and MTEL (Massachusetts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Program design should be informed by state licensure rules and MTEL objectives; Massachusetts lists subject-matter knowledge required for Math 5–8 (algebra, Euclidean geometry, trigonometry, discrete/finite mathematics, introductory calculus, history of mathematics) and additional topics for Math 8–12.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map course offerings to state-required topics and exam objectives; explicitly adopt course titles and content to match licensure subareas where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credit-hour and coursework minimums for licensure
rubrics_metrics.description: Massachusetts regulation: bachelor’s-degree initial license programs should take at least 36 credit hours of mathematics for Math 5–8 (need not be a major). For professional license a master's must contain at least 12 credits of graduate coursework in the field (historically required).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure program credit totals and distribution meet state requirements for the target license level; provide alternate tracks if candidates need pedagogy and practicum for initial licensure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program tracks and admission criteria (Salem MAT example)
rubrics_metrics.description: The M.A.T. is a 39-hour program with two tracks: professional (requires an initial license for admission; includes 9 math + 3 math-education courses + 3-credit clinical experience) and initial licensure (requires passing Middle School Mathematics MTEL by completion of first five math courses; includes additional pedagogy and student teaching).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer multiple tracks to serve practicing teachers seeking credential advancement and career-changers seeking initial licensure; clearly define admissions checkpoints (MTEL passage, existing licenses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Deep understanding as a program learning objective
rubrics_metrics.description: Deep understanding is defined as the ability to recognize multiple approaches, see similarities/differences, draw connections between concepts, and successfully communicate concepts to others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design coursework (discovery learning, problem solving, proofs, projects) to cultivate transferable conceptual flexibility rather than mechanical procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexible course formats and active learning methods
rubrics_metrics.description: No required format for courses; instructors have freedom to decide structure. Courses tend to have strong group-work components, discovery/hands-on activities, and may use lecture/discussion as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use small-class discussion, group discovery, experiments, manipulatives, software (Geometer’s Sketchpad, spreadsheets), and graphing calculators to foster active engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curriculum-connected assignments
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignments should link subject-matter to corresponding strands in state curriculum frameworks (e.g., Massachusetts Curriculum Frameworks) to make the relevance to middle school classroom explicit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require tasks that identify framework connections and explain classroom-level relevance; when content exceeds grade-level frameworks, emphasize how advanced mathematics deepens teacher understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of proofs and discrete mathematics to develop theorem-proving skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Program includes discrete mathematics and proof-writing in multiple courses to teach teachers to prove theorems and understand mathematical justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate proof tasks and discrete structures to build reasoning skills; include projects that require justification and explanation appropriate for future teachers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of manipulatives and physical experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples include shape blocks, geoboards, mirrors, Play-Doh experiments to approximate areas, dice/coin experiments, simulations on TI-84, and constructing Napier’s rods in history of mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ tangible activities to build intuition and to model pedagogical strategies teachers can use in middle grades classrooms.
